cycles.en_text_before_rewrite:
# I Thought It Was an AI Call—But There Was a Person Inside? Meta’s Unexpected Muse Test

Ring, ring... A call came from an AI agent. That was what it seemed. But while the conversation continued, the voice on the other end was not AI. It was a person.

Meta had run a test that produced exactly this kind of surprise.

The setting was the phone feature of Muse, an AI agent. In some calls made through Muse, trained contract workers, not AI, made the calls and carried the conversations through to the end.

It was like an AI costume: take it off, and a person steps out. Of course, having a person handle a call is not automatically bad. A person can take over when AI alone has trouble. As a system, that may even seem useful.

But then a problem appeared.

### What Callers Were Not Told

When contract workers handled calls, sensitive user information could be shared with call-center staff. People feel differently when they think they are speaking to a machine and when they know a person is listening. Names, plans, and private matters are easier to share when you know who is hearing them. The test began without explaining that contract staff might call.

This was where the story changed.

### The Reveal Behind the AI Sign

The reveal was not AI learning to sound human. A human was behind the AI sign. As AI makes calls and reservations, useful features make people want to know whether AI or a person is on the other end. A Meta executive called the undisclosed test a “mistake,” and the “human concierge” feature was rolled back for now.

## In one line

In the AI age, making a voice sound human is not enough: people must first be told who is on the other end.

deviations.claim_in_article: The headline says “I Thought It Was an AI Call,” and the opening says the call seemed to be from AI but the person on the other end was human; it adds that Meta’s test produced “exactly this kind of surprise.”
deviations.issue: The headline introduces a first-person experience, and the opening presents a particular recipient’s mistaken belief and surprise as an event produced by the test. The Japanese source evokes this scenario more tentatively; the Ledger verifies that trained contract staff handled some calls, but does not establish that a recipient believed a particular call was AI or was surprised.
deviations.explanation: The Ledger supports human-handled calls, but not this specific recipient’s belief or the claim that the test produced that exact surprise. The stronger, more definite framing is introduced in the adapted article.
same_fact_id_locations: Headline
Opening paragraphs beginning “Ring, ring...” and “Meta had run a test...”

deviations.claim_in_article: “People feel differently when they think they are speaking to a machine and when they know a person is listening.”
deviations.issue: This presents a general claim about people’s reactions. The Ledger records privacy concerns raised by Meta employees in the human-staff test; it does not establish this broader population-level claim.
deviations.explanation: The claim broadens test-specific employee concerns to people generally, a scope expansion also present in the Japanese source.
same_fact_id_locations: ### What Callers Were Not Told, paragraph beginning “When contract workers handled calls...”

deviations.claim_in_article: “Names, plans, and private matters are easier to share when you know who is hearing them.”
deviations.issue: This adds an unsupported claim that knowing who is listening makes personal information easier to share. The source says the listener’s identity matters, but does not make this causal claim.
deviations.explanation: The adapted wording adds a cause-and-effect claim about ease of sharing that is not in the Ledger or the Japanese source.
